Limited molecular flexibility (rotatable bonds ≤ 10) reduces the entropic penalty for adopting a membrane-permeable conformation. Adequate aqueous solubility ensures dissolution in GI fluids. Metabolic stability — resistance to CYP-mediated oxidation and Phase II conjugation — preserves the parent compound through first-pass metabolism.

Features associated with poor bioavailability: high MW (>500 Da) and excessive hydrogen bonding capacity reduce membrane permeability. Many rotatable bonds (>10) reduce the probability of adopting a compact, membrane-permeable conformation. Susceptibility to efflux by P-glycoprotein (Pgp) at the intestinal epithelium reduces net absorption. Labile metabolic soft spots — unhindered aromatic rings, benzylic positions, N-dealkylation sites — lead to rapid first-pass metabolism. Compounds that are substrates of CYP3A4 (the dominant gut-wall and hepatic CYP) face extensive first-pass extraction.
